cards.text: The {{c1::right}} heart pumps to the pulmonary (lesser) circulation; the {{c2::left}} heart to the systemic (greater) circulation.
cards.extra: Left works at far higher pressure → thicker wall.

cards.text: A vessel is named by flow direction, not oxygen: the pulmonary {{c1::artery}} carries deoxygenated blood, the pulmonary {{c2::veins}} carry oxygenated blood.
cards.extra: Artery leaves the heart; vein returns to it.

cards.text: The heart sits in the {{c1::middle}} mediastinum, wrapped by the pericardial sac.
cards.extra: Sternal angle splits mediastinum into superior and inferior.

cards.text: The heart is off-center: about {{c1::one third}} lies right of the midline and {{c2::two thirds}} to the left.
The heart's {{c1::base}} (superior/posterior) is formed by the atria and gives off the great vessels; the {{c2::apex}} (inferior/left) is the tip of the left ventricle.
The sternocostal (anterior) surface of the heart is mostly the {{c1::right ventricle}}; the right border is the {{c2::right atrium}}.
The coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus separates {{c1::atria from ventricles}}; the interventricular sulci mark the septum. Both carry the {{c2::coronary arteries}}.
The pericardium has an outer {{c1::fibrous}} layer (inelastic) and a {{c2::serous}} layer folded into parietal and visceral sheets; the visceral sheet on the heart is the {{c3::epicardium}}.
cards.extra: Pericardial cavity with lubricating fluid lies between the serous sheets.

cards.text: Because the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch, rapid fluid buildup compresses the heart: {{c1::cardiac tamponade}}.
The upper receiving chambers are the {{c1::atria}}; the lower pumping chambers are the {{c2::ventricles}}.
The left ventricular wall is far thicker because it pumps against the {{c1::systemic}} circulation (high pressure).
cards.extra: Wall thickness records the pressure load.

cards.text: The three cardiac wall layers, inside out, are {{c1::endocardium}}, {{c2::myocardium}} (~95% of thickness), and {{c3::epicardium}}.
Inside the ventricle, the trabeculae carneae and papillary muscles are {{c1::myocardium}}, but the chordae tendineae are {{c2::connective tissue}}.
cards.extra: Explains how the valve cannot evert.

cards.text: The right atrioventricular valve (RA→RV) is the {{c1::tricuspid}} valve, with {{c2::three}} cusps.
The left atrioventricular valve (LA→LV) is the {{c1::mitral (bicuspid)}} valve, with {{c2::two}} cusps.
In systole the papillary muscles pull the {{c1::chordae tendineae}}, holding the AV cusps so they do not collapse into the atrium.
cards.extra: Ruptured chord → cusp everts → regurgitation murmur.

cards.text: Which valves lack chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, sealing passively by their nest shape? {{c1::Semilunar (aortic and pulmonary)}}
cards.extra: Only the AV valves have that apparatus.

cards.text: The coronary ostia open behind the cusps of the {{c1::aortic}} valve, so the heart is perfused mainly in {{c2::diastole}}.
cards.extra: The heart feeds when it rests, not when it contracts.

cards.text: The fibrous skeleton anchors the valves, prevents orifice dilation, and {{c1::electrically insulates atria from ventricles}}.
cards.extra: Dense connective tissue, not bone; forces the impulse through one conduction point.

cards.text: The first heart sound is the closing of the {{c1::atrioventricular}} valves; the second, the closing of the {{c2::semilunar}} valves.
Venous blood of the heart is collected by the {{c1::coronary sinus}}, which empties directly into the {{c2::right atrium}}.
cards.extra: Large collector in the posterior coronary sulcus.

cards.text: From the aortic arch, on the right the {{c1::brachiocephalic trunk}} arises (splitting into right common carotid + right subclavian); on the left, the common carotid and subclavian arise {{c2::directly}}.
cards.extra: The brachiocephalic trunk exists only on the right.

cards.text: The superior and inferior venae cavae return systemic blood to the {{c1::right atrium}}; the four pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood to the {{c2::left atrium}}.
Direct arteriole-to-venule links that skip the capillary, the {{c1::arteriovenous anastomoses}}, serve mainly {{c2::temperature}} regulation.
cards.extra: Abundant in skin of extremities and mucosae.

cards.text: Most of the blood volume (~{{c1::64%}}) sits at any moment in the {{c2::venous}} system.
cards.extra: The vein is both return path and reservoir.

cards.text: The largest lymphatic vessel, the {{c1::thoracic duct}}, arises from the cisterna chyli and drains all but the {{c2::right upper quadrant}}.
The right upper quadrant is drained by the {{c1::right lymphatic duct}}; both ducts return lymph to the blood at the junction of the {{c2::subclavian and internal jugular}} veins.
Intestinal lymphatics ({{c1::lacteals}}) carry lipids and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), giving lymph a milky look called {{c2::chyle}}.
The lymphatic system is absent in the {{c1::CNS}}, {{c2::bone marrow}}, {{c3::cartilage}}, {{c4::bone}}, and {{c5::epithelia}} (epidermis, cornea).
